0.title: Course Introduction
0.content:
Welcome to the last lesson of Level 2! This is the final stop of a journey of taste — from Anjou's tuffeau stone, to Touraine's Cabernet Franc, to the Pineau d'Aunis of the tributary valleys, we have taken in the colourful face of the middle Loire all along the way. Now let a classic Touraine dish, "Rillettes de Tours," put the loveliest full stop on this journey, and then use the comprehensive assessment to confirm that you have truly mastered the essence of Level 2.

Learning Objectives

🍖 Understand the pairing logic of Chinon × Rillettes

Grasp why Cabernet Franc's acidity and tannin dance perfectly with French pork spread

📚 Consolidate all Level 2 knowledge

Review tuffeau geology, the three major Cabernet Franc AOCs, and the full picture of Touraine rosés and reds

🎓 Pass the Level 2 comprehensive assessment

Complete the quiz to confirm you have reached the knowledge level needed for Level 3
1.title: Rillettes de Tours — The Soul Dish of Touraine
1.content:
Rillettes de Tours is one of France's most famous pork spreads, ranking alongside Rillettes du Mans as one of France's two traditional rillettes; the Touraine version is known for its finer texture and richer lard character.

🍖 What are rillettes?

Pork shoulder, belly or duck is slow-cooked in its own fat at a very low temperature (70–80°C) for hours, then shredded into fine strands with a fork, mixed with the melted fat, and cooled into a dense spreadable texture. Traditionally eaten spread on toasted bread.

🏆 Tours vs Mans

  • Rillettes de Tours IGP: darker in colour, denser in texture, with more obvious fat and a richer pork flavour
  • Rillettes du Mans: paler in colour, looser in texture, with more lard, and smoother

Both are best paired with French sparkling wine or Chinon, but the heavy fattiness of Rillettes de Tours needs a high-acid wine to balance it.
2.title: Chinon × Rillettes: The Science of a Perfect Pairing
2.highlights.0.title: Acidity cuts fat
2.highlights.0.content: Cabernet Franc's high acidity (typically pH 3.4–3.6) effectively cuts the rich fat of rillettes, so each sip resets the palate
2.highlights.1.title: Low tannin doesn't clash
2.highlights.1.content: The supple tannins of Loire Cabernet Franc (lower than Bordeaux versions) don't produce astringency with pork protein, but complement it instead
2.highlights.2.title: Floral-fruity notes lift the dish
2.highlights.2.content: Chinon's violet and red-berry aromas complement the salty meat flavour of rillettes, creating a layered "sweet–salty contrast"
2.content:
Food pairing is not arbitrary — behind it lie strict scientific and sensory logic. Chinon × Rillettes is the most classic example of a Loire pairing:

Pairing chemistry analysis

The challenge: rillettes' main characteristics are high fat (lard) and high salt, plus protein-rich pork fibres — all three need a specific response from the wine.

The solution:

  • Fat → needs acidity to cut it (Cabernet Franc's crisp high acidity ✓)
  • Salt → slightly sweet fruit (Chinon's raspberry fruit) lifts the savoury layers ✓
  • Protein → needs a moderate amount of tannin (but not too high, or it turns astringent) ✓

This is why New World Cabernets that overemphasise oak and tannin don't suit rillettes, while the light Loire versions are just right.

🍽️ Extended pairings — Level 2 AOCs × Touraine dishes

  • 🍷 Saumur-Champigny + Rilettes de Tours — the most classic combination
  • 🥩 Chinon Coteau (older vintages) + Gigot d'agneau (roast leg of lamb)
  • 🐔 Bourgueil + Poulet rôti (butter-roasted chicken) + thyme
  • 🌹 Rosé-de-Loire + Rillons de Touraine (fried pork belly)
  • 🐖 Touraine-Noble-Joué + Charcuterie platter (French cold-cut platter)
3.title: Level 2 Knowledge Map Review
3.content:
🪨 L2-1: Tuffeau geology

  • Porous white limestone, good drainage, can be dug into underground cellars
  • Western Anjou: schist (retains heat, strongly mineral)
  • Eastern Saumur: tuffeau (crisp and light)
  • Climate transition from maritime in the west to semi-continental in the east

🍷 L2-2: Anjou-Saumur reds

  • Anjou Rouge → Anjou-Villages → Anjou-Brissac (three levels)
  • Saumur-Champigny: top Cabernet Franc from the tuffeau plateau, the Clos Rougeard legend
  • Varieties: Cabernet Franc-led, a little Cabernet Sauvignon

🌹 L2-3: Anjou rosé spectrum

  • Rosé-de-Loire (dry, Cab. Franc ≥30%)
  • Cabernet-d'Anjou (off-dry, 10–40 g/L)
  • Rosé-d'Anjou (off-dry, Grolleau-led)
  • Haut-Poitou (promoted 2011, Sauvignon Blanc whites)

🏰 L2-4: The Cabernet Franc triangle

  • Chinon: three soils (gravel, tuffeau slopes, clay plateau)
  • Bourgueil: mixed tuffeau and gravel, weighty structure
  • Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil: sandy gravel, lightest and most floral

🎭 L2-5: The full picture of Touraine reds

  • Touraine Rouge: Gamay + Cabernet Franc + Côt
  • Touraine-Amboise: beside the Château d'Amboise
  • Touraine-Noble-Joué: a unique AOC that must blend 3 Pinots (one of France's most unusual)

🌶️ L2-6: Tributary reds

  • Pineau d'Aunis: white-pepper spice, almost only in the Loire
  • Coteaux-du-Loir and Coteaux-du-Vendômois: the heartland of Pineau d'Aunis
  • Orléans/Orléans-Cléry: the northernmost AOCs, a natural-wine stronghold
4.title: Level 2 Comprehensive Assessment (Question 1)
4.highlights.0.content: An IGP-certified Touraine pork spread, dense in texture and heavy in fat, the traditional pairing for Chinon
4.highlights.1.title: The science of pairing
4.highlights.1.content: Food pairing must consider the interaction of four dimensions: acidity, tannin, sweetness and aroma
4.quiz.question: What is the main reason the Chinon × Rillettes de Tours pairing works?
4.quiz.options.0: Rich tannins can wrap and balance the pork fat
4.quiz.options.1: Cabernet Franc's high acidity effectively cuts the pork fat, and its supple tannins don't clash with the protein
4.quiz.options.2: Low acidity makes the fat rounder without clashing
4.quiz.options.3: Sweetness complements the saltiness of rillettes in a sweet–salty match
4.quiz.explanation: Cabernet Franc's high acidity (pH 3.4–3.6) effectively cuts the rich fat of rillettes, "resetting" the palate after each sip. At the same time the supple tannins of Loire Cabernet Franc (lower than Bordeaux versions) do not produce astringency with the pork protein, so the two complement each other perfectly.
5.title: Level 2 Comprehensive Assessment (Question 2)
5.highlights.0.title: The Touraine AOC system
5.highlights.0.content: Touraine includes several sub-AOCs, each with its own variety and style rules
5.highlights.1.title: The three Pinot brothers
5.highlights.1.content: A certain French AOC requires Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier to be blended together
5.quiz.question: Which of the following AOCs requires a blend of three Pinot varieties (Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier)?
5.quiz.explanation: Touraine-Noble-Joué is one of France's most unique AOCs, requiring a blend of the three Pinot varieties Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier, in regulated proportions, producing a rosé with floral aromas and fine acidity. This is the special rule most worth memorising in Level 2, and the best representative of the Loire's varietal diversity.
6.title: Level 2 Comprehensive Assessment (Question 3)
6.highlights.0.content: The Loire's most distinctive native red variety, found almost only in the tributary regions
6.highlights.1.title: Aroma identification
6.highlights.1.content: Each variety has a unique aromatic fingerprint, an important clue in blind tasting
6.quiz.question: What is the most typical aroma characteristic of Pineau d'Aunis?
6.quiz.options.0: Tropical fruit (passion fruit, mango) and white flowers
6.quiz.options.2: White-pepper spice with fresh red berries
6.quiz.explanation: Pineau d'Aunis' signature aroma is an intense white-pepper spice (rather than black pepper), with fresh red berries (raspberry, cranberry). This variety is found almost only in the Loire's tributary regions such as Coteaux-du-Loir and Coteaux-du-Vendômois, and is an important point for variety identification in Level 2.
